Leader’s Report on XXV Indian Scientific 
Expedition to Antarctica—An Overview
L. Prem Kishore
Leader XXV ISEA
“Antarctica is suspended between two ages -  those of competitive 
nationalism and cooperative internationalism — Alan K. Herikson.
Antarctica continent, comprising almost 10% of the land surface of 
the globe, is linked to the vast extent of the Southern Ocean surrounding it. 
Remote from all centers of population it has no indigenous people living 
there. Antarctica the last heritage of mankind and the continent of extremes, 
has come to be known as the “Continent of Science”. The white desert 
Antarctica is a pristine and natural laboratory, enabling the scientists to 
study, detect and monitor global phenomena, such as those related to 
atmospheric, meteorological parameter, oceanographic and glaciological, 
geological and geophysical research which may provide clue to the 
evolutionary history of the continents and the Paleo-climate of the earth.
Patterns of Antarctica Science and Adventure had been set in the 
early eighties in the context of Indian Antarctic Programme. Our continuous 
pursuance of science has been the driving force for the successful launching 
of the annual scientific expeditions to Antarctica every year since 1981 
and the maintenance of year round permanent station Maitri is the testimony 
to the India’s commitment to Antarctic Research. Indian Antarctic 
Programme has marched towards the Silver Jubilee expedition and it is a 
matter of happy coincidence that the silver jubilee celebrations of Indian 
Antarctic programme coincides with the International Polar Year Campaign.
Indian Antarctic Programme is multi-disciplinary and multi- 
institutional involving major themes focused on Meteorology and 
Atmospheric Sciences, Earth Sciences and Glaciology, Biology and 
Environmental Sciences, Human Physiology and Medicines and 
Engineering and Communications and Polar Logistics.
Humans do not belong to Antarctica. They go there like Astronauts 
entering deep space, taking with them everything needed for survival, i.e. 
accommodation, food and fuel. Every visitor is a transient, staying for 
limited periods, a few weeks or months, or wintering for a whole year. No

6 L. Prem Kishore
one lives indefinitely in Antarctica. Each expedition not only works in and 
copes with a mercilessly hostile environment but has to endure raw realities 
of human interaction in isolation, with attendant passions, personal 
idiosyncrasies, occasional medical emergencies and some grinding routine. 
The evolving importance of Antarctic Science is the changing emphasis 
from exploiting resources to conservation and new awareness ot the 
importance of Antarctica in assessing global climate change.
Launching
The members of the 25th Silver Jubilee Indian Scientific Expedition 
to Antarctica assembled at National Centre for Antarctica & Ocean 
Research (NCAOR), Goa on 16th December 2005. A hearty and warm 
welcome was given by Dr S. Rajan, Dr M. Sudhakar, and Dr N. Khare. The 
team comprised of few experienced members of the past expeditions, 
budding enthusiastic youngsters and a contingent of Officers and other 
ranks from the Indian Army with the spirit of the expedition, zeal and 
enthusiasm. The same day the Insurance and other formalities were 
completed and the next four days up to 20th December 2005 were very 
hectic for the members with many activities, orientation lecturers and the 
Launching. A chronology of the happenings, activities and events till the 
sailing is briefly given below.
A visit to M/s Sea Scan Marine Services Pvt. Ltd. Panaji was organized 
for giving essential training in Fire Fighting, Fire Prevention and Personal 
Survival Techniques. Both theories as well as practical demonstrations were 
given. This is very important for the members who venture out for an 
expedition to Antarctica where fire hazards are the foremost concern and 
principal danger at all Antarctic stations. There are detailed established 
procedures for fire prevention and fire fighting in Antarctica which every 
participating member should be well versed with.
Orientation lectures by eminent personalities on various topics were 
organized. Lectures on Utilities and up-keep of Maitri Station by 
Dr. S. Mukerji, Medical care by Dr. S.C. Tiwari, Environmental protocols 
by Shri Rasik Ravindra and Psychological aspects by Dr. Manju Mehta 
were action-packed and informative. These lectures provided the members 
the required knowledge, the inspiration and confidence to take up the 
challenges and tasks ahead of them.

Necessary instructions were given by Dr. N. Khare and Mr. P. Shetkar 
on various aspects of the submission of data acquired during the expedition 
at Antarctica to the National Antarctica Data Centre.
